1:
The steward’s motive is read the same way by everyone, and read back from the sequel. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) has him not content to be manager but longing to be master of the estate, fishing in troubled waters, since a grant from the crown would serve him whichever side won; the present was timed to incline the king to him, a man’s gift making room for him before great men. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) says he grossly slandered his master, doubtless for personal gain, and draws a harder inference still: he shows an entire want of principle, and can therefore have adhered to David’s cause only because he had the shrewdness to foresee its ultimate success. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) put it plainly as calumny in the hope of getting possession of the lands he was farming for his master. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) does not argue but exclaims, asking what a base wretch this was and how unfounded the accusation against a peaceable and innocent man.

The present itself is explained, and how its itemising should be taken is disputed. Clarke corrects the English: the word loaf gives a false idea of ancient Jewish bread, which was thin cakes and not yeasted and raised like ours; the summer fruits were probably cucumbers or watermelons, used in those countries to refresh travellers in the burning heat, which Harmer supposes is why they are called summer fruits; and the bottle was a goat’s skin, the general vessel of the East. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) adds only that it was a large one, proportionable to the rest of the provisions. On the apportioning Clarke reads a formula rather than a plan: it is the Eastern manner of speaking when anything is presented to a great man, that this and this is for the slaves of the servants of your majesty, when the presents are meant for the sovereign himself and are so understood — a compliment amounting to the claim that they are not worthy of his acceptance. Keil and Delitzsch take the allocation literally, the asses for the king’s family to ride in turn, the bread and fruit for the servants, the wine for those who should faint in the desert, and note the written form of one word to be a copyist’s error. Henry takes it literally too and makes a point of the wine, meant for the faint and not for the king or his courtiers: blessed is the land whose princes use wine for strength, as David did, and not for drunkenness, as Absalom did.

On the judgment that followed all six converge, and the agreement is the finding. Henry holds that David knew the man was not ambitious but easy in his place, nor could expect with his lame legs to climb the ladder of preferment; yet he credited the calumny and without further enquiry convicted him of treason and granted away his lands — a rash judgment of which he was afterwards ashamed. Ellicott calls the story almost too improbable to be believed, since a helpless cripple of Saul’s house could hardly have hoped the rebellion would bring him the throne; but David, apt to be hasty in his judgments, was in a state to believe any tale of ingratitude and deeply affected by so large a contribution to his necessities. Keil and Delitzsch add that the man had never put in any claim to the throne before, and conclude that in the excited state he was then in the king was weak enough to credit it and commit the injustice. John Gill (reformed) is the most measured: had the charge been true the forfeiture would have been righteous, the lands having been forfeited once already by Ishbosheth’s rebellion and graciously restored, yet it seems too hasty a step to give them away without further inquiry.
5:
What blood the curse meant is canvassed and left open. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) say outright that it cannot be determined with certainty, and allow that Shimei may have laid the deaths of Ishbosheth and Abner to David’s charge, innocent though he was of both. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) doubts whether more was meant than holding him responsible for the blood of Saul’s house, instancing those deaths and the execution of Saul’s seven descendants at the Gibeonites’ demand. John Gill (reformed) calls the insinuations false, as if David had stirred up the Philistines to the battle in which Saul fell. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) offers the same alternatives, and three notice independently that the giving up of the seven sons, though related later in the book, seems to have happened before this.

Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) sets the scene against the one before it: David bore these curses much better than the steward’s flatteries, since by the flatteries he passed a wrong judgment on another and by the curses a right judgment on himself — the world’s smiles, he concludes, being more dangerous than its frowns. He gives reasons why the moment was chosen: that it now seemed safe, though it would have cost the man his life had the king resented it, and that David’s distress seemed to make Providence endorse the reproach — the principle on which Job’s friends condemned him. He notes that the dust thrown would blow back into the thrower’s eyes, as causeless curses return on their author’s head.

The rebuff of Abishai is read two ways. Keil and Delitzsch take the formula about the sons of Zeruiah to signify that a man wished nothing in common with another’s feelings and views, and suppose Joab had joined his brother; Gill supposes the same and offers a choice of senses — either a refusal of their counsel, or the question what is it to me or to you, since the cursing will hurt neither. Wesley gives the first sense flatly: in this matter I ask not your advice, nor will I follow it.

That the Lord had bidden Shimei curse is the hard saying, and each witness reaches for a different instrument. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) works on the particle, which should be rendered not because but for if — for if the Lord hath said unto him, Curse David, who shall then say, Wherefore hast thou done so? He adds that no soul of man can suppose God ever bade one man curse another, this being a peculiarity of the Hebrew, which does not always distinguish permission from commandment. Wesley works on providence: God put no wickedness into Shimei’s heart, which was of itself full of malignity, but left him to it and brought David so low that he might seem a proper object of scorn — ground enough for an expression that speaks not by the word of his precept but of his providence. Ellicott works on David’s intention: he does not justify the wrong, but holds that so far as it bears on himself it is of divine appointment and not to be resented. Keil and Delitzsch work on the text, holding the written form to mean upon the guilt that really belongs to me, the word never meaning misery. Henry works on the distinction between the act and the affliction: as Shimei’s sin it was not from God but from his own wicked heart, and God’s hand in it neither excused nor extenuated it, any more than it did the sin of those who put Christ to death; but as David’s affliction it was from the Lord. He adds the mechanism the others leave out: of Saul’s blood David’s conscience acquitted him, but it charged him with the blood of Uriah, so the reproach was too true though false as the man meant it.
15:
How the question to Hushai should be heard divides them. John Gill (reformed) has Absalom put it not in displeasure but overjoyed that so trusty a friend of his father’s had deserted him, and only to try his integrity; he notes that Absalom will not name David, nor give him his title, nor own the relation of father, but says merely thy friend, and could not charge ingratitude without reproaching himself. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) agrees it was said only to try him, and reads the phrase as a reflection on David, a friend to strangers but not to his own son, whom by his severity he had provoked — and so he does not vouchsafe to call him his father. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) has him surprised instead, and inclined to distrust a man who had deserted his master.

The answer is read as craft, as principle, and as equivocation. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) call it great craftiness that Hushai declared at the outset that Jehovah had chosen Absalom — at least, they add, he could come to no other conclusion judging from the results. Ellicott makes it an argument rather than a trick: Hushai rests his conduct on loyalty to the government in fact, urges that this has divine authority, and offers his past faithfulness as a pledge of faithfulness now. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) names it an equivocation: Hushai meant in his heart that God and Israel had chosen David, but spoke so as to make Absalom believe he spoke of him — and whatever insincerity appears in it, Hushai is alone answerable.

Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) frames the pair as one ruin: Absalom thought himself sure of success in having the two most celebrated politicians of the age, relying on them and not on the ark, though he had it with him — yet miserable counsellors were they both, the one an enemy who would never counsel him to do wisely, the other counselling him to do wickedly and so betraying him as effectually as the man who meant to. A government founded in sin, Henry adds, is founded on sand. He observes too that the greatest politicians often act most foolishly for themselves, this one cried up as an oracle yet throwing in with a rash youth whose fall he of all men might have foreseen.

On the counsel itself the reasoning is agreed and the motive is not. Keil and Delitzsch call the advice sagacious enough: to take the royal harem was to appropriate the throne, making reconciliation impossible and so binding Absalom’s followers the more firmly to his cause. Ellicott adds that taking a predecessor’s harem was an Oriental custom to whose enormity the mind was blunted by polygamy. Wesley adds a private motive: that Ahithophel acted partly to revenge the injury done to Bathsheba, the daughter of his own son — which Henry also reports, as what some think. Clarke calls it an infernal measure, notes that a conquered king’s wives were always the conqueror’s property and that Herodotus reports Smerdis espousing all his predecessor’s, but insists that for a son to take his father’s was the sum of abomination and death by the law, rarely found even among the Gentiles.

Three witnesses independently make the place the point. Clarke thinks it was done on the very spot where David’s eye had taken its adulterous view; Gill says it was the spot from which he had the sight of Bathsheba; Ellicott observes that Nathan had foretold the public punishment should answer the secret crime, and finds it striking that it falls on the very roof where David first yielded. Keil and Delitzsch close with the historian’s own account, that this counsel was in those days with both father and son as if a man had enquired of the word of God.
